sentences.sentence: You seemed upset and agitated, throwing up your arms while you waited for your turn in line.
Complaining loudly, you brushed my mother aside, “I’ll pay for her.” You barked the words with a ferocity that startled everyone nearby.
I looked at Mom who made a quiet, resigned face, but she said nothing, just folded her hands under her scarf and waited.

You weren’t a hero—the way people pretended you were, with those soft, admiring glances at the coffee shop counter, the way strangers tried to pat your back or say, “Go on, champ, show them what you got.” I didn’t see it.
You never had, not really.
You just got angry, and sometimes, when you weren’t, you still acted like you did, like the world depended on you.
The girl—she came in after you, clutching a tattered notebook and looking up as you finished your transaction and turned to go.
She didn’t come over with the eager heroism of the other kids, but something about her eyes made you slow down.
She said nothing, just stared for a beat before opening her mouth.
“Actually,” she said softly, “you *are* a hero.
Not because of what you do, but because you notice things.”
Your fists unclenched just a little.
Maybe that’s why you liked her.
She smiled, small but sincere.
“Because even when you’re frustrated, you help someone else see they don’t have to be alone.”
You didn’t know what to say.
Maybe that was true.
Maybe you were a hero for reasons nobody else could see.

sentences.sentence: PT 2
I leaned my rifle against the bed and put my backpack on, and as I was reaching for my rifle again the whole house rocked and I heard a series of impacts in every direction.
More landing pods, of course.
If the sirens had been any louder, I’d think the building was under attack—not just from above, but from within the walls themselves.
The communication crackled in the background: “This is 911.
We already know.
Arm yourself and lock your doors.
Good luck and God bless.” Static, then silence.
My heart hammered in my chest as I checked the door.
It was already chained from the inside; the auto-lock was engaged.
I could feel the tension in my fingers, knuckles white as I tried to steady myself.
Outside, through the reinforced glass, the sky was now a web of red and white—enemy signals flashing like angry eyes.
I heard shouting, but it was muffled, garbled through the walls.
My neighbor’s door next door was blown in, splinters dancing across the hallway.
The hum of the security grid powered down—so I had seconds to move.
The floorboards creaked as I hurried to the stairwell, rifle cradled close.
As I pressed my back against the cold metal rail, another explosion rattled the building.
We weren’t supposed to be prepared for this.
No one told us what to do if they came for us while we were still asleep, arms at our sides.
But I had listened.
I had locked my door.
And I had grabbed my rifle.
I took one last look at the battered hallway behind me, the splintered remains of the bedroom door—partially open, its chain smoldering.
My reflection warred with the shadow moving in the stairwell’s gloom.

sentences.sentence: He heard the shouting before he saw them coming.
God took one look out the window and groaned.
He reached for his aspirin — it had earned a spot in every room he owned — and plodded downstairs to the foyer.
The air was thick with the metallic tang of spilled blood and burnt incense, like a cathedral abandoned mid-catharsis.
The grand doors had been propped open, inviting the chaos within.
Across the threshold stood the new batch.
Humanity, as he’d designed them: sinewy, sharp-toothed, eyes glinting with that uncanny mix of hunger and cunning.
They looked less like the favored children of creation and more like failed prototypes from other gods' workshops, their skins marked by scars earned in endless gladiatorial games.
Even now, some were still shaking off the haze of battle, muttering prayers to gods long dead or new gods that hadn’t yet taken an interest.
He sipped his tea, grimacing at the taste of regret.
Natural selection had worked better than he’d ever thought.
He’d built them to compete, to adapt, to survive at all costs.
But he hadn’t quite expected… this spectacle.

These games, staged in his marble courtyard, where humans fought for the favor of wagering deities — each tournament a challenge thrown down between the old gods and their chosen species, with humanity thrown in to gamble their fate.
One of the fighters staggered past, covered in blood but grinning wildly.
His eyes met God’s in the doorway.
“Why do they keep coming?” the human rasped.
“Why us?”
God hesitated.
He wanted to explain, to apologize, to tell them this was a test — but his voice always sounded so… thin, so distant to them.

sentences.sentence: (First timer here, be gentle!
Sorry it's a little long.)
I'm still not certain exactly how it happened, but to be honest, I'm okay with that.

All I know is that one minute I was driving home after a long shift at the office, the next minute I was sitting at a corner table in a coffee shop, staring in utter bewilderment at a tiny figure wearing a dark suit—and a lot of coffee creamer.
It surprised me how much creamer Death put in his coffee.
The glass jar looked comically full from the other side of the counter.
I mean, it *was* Death.
The very Death.
Rake-nosed, skeletal, those shadowy eyes that made my skin prickle even over my scarf.
You’d think someone who represented the end of things would be… minimalist.
But here he was, stirring a cup with a spoon and adding what looked like a double shot of vanilla creamer.
Was it his idea?
Did he find it comforting?
I hesitated at the counter, my own coffee cold and untouched.
The barista looked just as stunned.
Death raised his bony fingers in a gesture that might have been a wave.
“You don’t have to be scared,” he said, his voice rumbling but oddly gentle, like distant thunder.
“Not if you’re with company.” He gave a toothy grin that somehow radiated warmth.
I found myself fumbling for my phone and pulling up the news—just to make sure I hadn’t blacked out somehow.
But my phone was dead.
The street outside was blurred by my tears, or maybe it was fear.
I sipped my own coffee, which had been black for fifteen minutes, and Death sipped with the quiet reverence of someone who knew how flavor was earned, not wasted.

sentences.sentence: ‘I figure you should be twenty one by now.’ The words on the page tremble slightly as I try and read.
If not, I suppose I should complain to the postal service—after all, I paid good money to make sure this got here on time.
The return address is spidery, ink faded but unmistakable: my brother, Sam.
Seventeen years, just like he said in his final letter.
He was always the prankster, the one who’d send me things from strange places and keep promises, even when he didn’t think he could.
The box looks exactly as he described—a wooden puzzle box with the words "Only for the cleverest sibling" scratched across the lid.
Inside, instead of the pieces, there's a black-and-white photograph of us as kids, grinning with braces and scraped knees.
The back of the photo has been taped over with scrawled writing: *You didn’t solve it, but I still know you did it in your heart.
I stare at my hands, too large now for the games we used to play together.
I remember when he said goodbye, how he pressed something into my palm before… before he left.
I’d never found it.
But here it is, right in front of me, heavy with meaning.
I open the little latch.

sentences.sentence: I knew it.
I fucking knew it.
I knew it as soon as he put it in my hand.
He’d just slammed the lid back down on the burrito like it was a cheap takeout container, and the heat rushed up my arm like a warning shot.
He laughed at his own joke—I still remember the way he shrugged, all smug and practiced.
That was the thing about Juan: his hands were always moving, but his thought process was lazy.
He’d said, “You want the extra heat?
No?
Cool.” and just shoved the folded tortilla at me.
I should have just eaten it, really.
Closed my eyes, taken a huge bite, let the spice burn everything else away.
But my hand had moved on its own.
Something primal, deep in my bones.
I gripped the burrito not to rip it open, but to twist it—fingertips finding the seam, pressing against the edges.
I didn’t know why I did it.
Maybe the boredom, the way he talked so fast, not even listening, the familiar texture of the rice and meat under my thumb.
Maybe it was rage.
Maybe I just needed to know.
So I did what my body demanded: I ripped it open, steam curling into my face.
And that’s when it happened.

sentences.sentence: I remember my first days as a doctor.
I wore my stethoscope proudly around my neck, not realizing it also marked me as somewhat of an outsider—even more so than I realized.
In the hospital corridors, the seasoned physicians nodded grudgingly at Dr. Agon, the eager but green-eyed intern they'd all once been.
I introduced myself as Dr. Agon, and tried to sound confident while my hands shook.
I’d rehearsed scripts for every scenario, yet in real life, panic and curiosity tangled together in my chest like a double helix.
I prided myself on kindness—listening to every patient, taking notes in the margins of charts, speaking softly when they did.
But I didn't realize how little the world could survive when guided only by compassion and an overblown sense of purpose.
I chased the miracle, the instant when disease would yield to my touch.
Sometimes I healed, but other times, my interventions were too desperate, too inexperienced, too easy to manipulate.
One day, I met a man named Viktor—older, a former spy with haunted eyes and scars the chart couldn't explain.
He was in there for a heart condition, but he was also there for something else: unfinished business.
Maybe guilt.
Maybe revenge.
I saw an opportunity to make a difference.
I prescribed him stronger medication than the guidelines suggested, justified it as “aggressive therapy,” though my heart told me it was a risk.
Viktor stared at me with those dark eyes and nodded, understanding more than I could know.

sentences.sentence: Well, Mr.
What do you say to this?
You flick your tail with annoyance, ears flattened.
I've done it, you think.
After all these years—late nights, empty coffee cups, and stacks of microscopes.
I’ve got the proof.
The proof that your purrs are not just cat noises, but codes.
That the way you sit in the sun in Mrs. Kline’s garden?
That’s not leisure.
That’s transmission.
I shove the envelope across the table.
A few papers spill out, catching the fluorescent light.
There are sketches, blurry satellite images, notes labeled "Phase 1," "Signal Intake," and a photo of you, Mr. Fluffykins, sitting next to a suspiciously wire-caged bird cage in the pound.
And another—*you* at a piano, looking strangely contemplative as a digital screen blinks above your whiskers.
I lean in.
"See this?
These photographs were taken at exact intervals.
The patterns in your eyes— synchronizing with clock signals from satellites.
